title: System Design Handbook
summary: Your quick review companion: match symptoms to fixes, check useful numbers, compare technologies, choose consistency and spot interview red flags.
body:
## How to use this handbook

Use this page to refresh what you have learned, not to learn everything at once. Each row points to an idea covered in a full lesson. If one feels unfamiliar, follow its link (paths look like `/system-design/<slug>`) and practise it before your interview. Here are three ways to use the handbook:

- **Night before:** skim the master table and the numbers. Say each trade-off column out loud.
- **During practice:** when you get stuck in a deep dive, find the symptom in the master table and ask which fix fits *this* requirement.
- **After practice:** check your design against the red-flags list at the end.

A fix is only correct when it is tied to a requirement. "Add Kafka" is not an answer; "writes arrive in 10x bursts during sales, so a queue absorbs the burst while workers drain at the database's sustained rate" is.

> **Common mix-up: caches do not scale writes, queues do not scale reads.** Caches, read replicas and CDNs *scale reads*: they serve copies so the primary sees fewer reads. They add work to every write (invalidation, replication). Queues help *writes* only by absorbing bursts and moving work off the request path; if the sustained arrival rate exceeds what consumers and the database can absorb, the backlog grows forever. Raising sustained write capacity needs sharding/partitioning, batching or a write-optimized store.

## Interview delivery checklist

Follow the same order every time so you never forget a step. Budget for a 45-minute round; scale proportionally for 60.

| Step | 45 min | 60 min | Output you should have on the board |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Functional requirements | 3–4 min | 5 min | 3 core "users can…" items, explicit out-of-scope list |
| 2. Non-functional requirements | 2–3 min | 4 min | Scale, latency target, availability vs consistency *per operation*, durability |
| 3. Estimates (only if they change a decision) | 0–3 min | 0–4 min | Peak QPS, storage growth, read:write ratio |
| 4. Core entities | 2 min | 3 min | 3–6 nouns with key fields |
| 5. API | 4–5 min | 5 min | One endpoint per functional requirement, auth and pagination noted |
| 6. High-level design | 10–12 min | 14 min | A working baseline that satisfies every functional requirement |
| 7. Deep dives | 12–15 min | 20 min | 2–3 non-functional requirements made true, with trade-offs |
| 8. Wrap-up | 2 min | 3 min | Bottlenecks, what you would monitor, what you would build next |

Get a small, complete design on the board before optimizing it. Guide the conversation, but leave room for feedback: "I'll move to the API unless you want more on requirements." Whenever you add a component, explain what it buys you and what it costs.

## Problem → standard fixes (master table)

Find the symptom, pick the fix that matches the requirement, and say the trade-off.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S["Bottleneck found"] --> R{"Reads or writes?"}
    R -->|"Reads"| R1{"Same data read often?"}
    R1 -->|"Yes"| C["Cache or CDN"]
    R1 -->|"No, spread out"| RR["Read replicas"]
    R1 -->|"Expensive query"| P["Precompute or search index"]
    R -->|"Writes"| W1{"Bursty or sustained?"}
    W1 -->|"Bursty"| Q["Queue to absorb burst"]
    W1 -->|"Sustained"| W2{"One hot key?"}
    W2 -->|"Yes"| K["Salt or split the key"]
    W2 -->|"No"| SH["Shard, batch, or LSM store"]
```

Start by classifying the bottleneck. Read problems branch on access pattern: repeated reads of the same data favour a cache or CDN, broadly spread reads favour replicas, and expensive queries favour precomputation or a purpose-built index. Write problems branch on shape: bursts can be smoothed with a queue, while sustained overload needs more write capacity through sharding, batching or a write-optimized store, after first checking for a single hot key.

### Scale and throughput

| Problem | Symptom / signal | Standard fixes | Trade-off to mention | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scale reads | High read:write ratio (10:1 to 1000:1); primary CPU or IOPS saturated by SELECTs | Cache-aside (Redis/Memcached); read replicas; CDN for static/public content; denormalize or precompute views; search index for text/filter queries | Staleness and invalidation; replica lag breaks read-your-writes; cache stampede on hot-key expiry | [pattern-scaling-reads](/system-design/pattern-scaling-reads) |
| Scale writes | Primary write IOPS/WAL saturated; lock contention; write latency rising with load | Shard/partition by a high-cardinality key; queue to absorb bursts; batch and coalesce writes; LSM/write-optimized store (Cassandra, RocksDB-based); salt hot keys | Cross-shard queries and transactions get hard; resharding cost; a queue adds latency and only buys time if sustained rate exceeds capacity | [pattern-scaling-writes](/system-design/pattern-scaling-writes) |
| Hot key / celebrity | One partition at 100% while others idle; one cache node melts | Replicate hot read keys across nodes or add a local in-process cache; split hot write keys into N sub-keys and sum on read; fan-out on read for celebrities | Reads of split keys cost N lookups; detection needs per-key metrics | [sharding-and-partitioning](/system-design/sharding-and-partitioning) |
| Counting at scale | Millions of increments/sec to a few counters; exact distinct counts too costly | Sharded counters; stream aggregation (Kafka + Flink) into time windows; HyperLogLog for distinct counts (~0.8% error in ~12 KB in Redis); count-min sketch for heavy hitters | Approximate answers; windowing and late events need a policy; reconcile with batch job if money is involved | [design-top-k-heavy-hitters](/system-design/design-top-k-heavy-hitters) |

### Data movement and work

| Problem | Symptom / signal | Standard fixes | Trade-off to mention | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Large files | Uploads/downloads of MB–GB passing through app servers; timeouts on big requests | Presigned URL so the client uploads directly to blob storage; multipart / resumable (chunked) upload; CDN for downloads; store metadata in DB, bytes in blob | Metadata and blob can disagree (need upload-complete callback or event); presigned URLs must expire and be scoped | [pattern-handling-large-blobs](/system-design/pattern-handling-large-blobs) |
| Long-running jobs | Request takes seconds to hours (transcoding, reports, crawling) | Accept → return job ID (202) → queue → worker pool → status polling or webhook; persist job state | Need retries, visibility timeouts and idempotent workers; poison messages need a dead-letter queue | [pattern-long-running-tasks](/system-design/pattern-long-running-tasks) |
| Multi-step workflows | Several services must all succeed (pay, reserve, ship) | Saga with compensating actions; durable workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions); transactional outbox to publish events atomically with DB writes | No global ACID; intermediate states are visible; compensations must be idempotent | [pattern-multi-step-processes](/system-design/pattern-multi-step-processes) |
| Real-time updates | Users must see changes within ~1 s (chat, live scores, driver location) | Short polling → long polling → SSE (server→client) → WebSocket (bidirectional); pub/sub fan-out between servers; fan-out on write vs on read for feeds | Stateful connections complicate load balancing and deploys; must catch up missed messages on reconnect | [pattern-real-time-updates](/system-design/pattern-real-time-updates) |

### Correctness under concurrency and failure

| Problem | Symptom / signal | Standard fixes | Trade-off to mention | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Contention / double booking | Two users grab the last seat; overselling inventory | DB transaction + `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`; optimistic concurrency with a version column; atomic conditional update (`UPDATE … WHERE status='free'`); reservation with TTL hold; distributed lock with fencing token (only when the resource spans systems) | Pessimistic locks hurt throughput under high contention; optimistic retries thrash on hot rows; locks without fencing are unsafe after GC pauses | [pattern-managing-contention](/system-design/pattern-managing-contention) |
| Exactly-once-ish processing | Retries cause duplicate charges, emails or counts | Client idempotency key + dedupe table with unique constraint; idempotent consumers; transactional outbox; upserts | Exactly-once delivery is not achievable end to end; you get at-least-once delivery plus idempotent effects | [idempotency-and-delivery-guarantees](/system-design/idempotency-and-delivery-guarantees) |
| Unreliable dependencies | Slow downstream causes thread exhaustion and cascading failure | Timeouts on every call; retries with exponential backoff + jitter (only for idempotent ops); circuit breaker; bulkheads (separate pools); backpressure and load shedding | Retries amplify load (retry storms); breakers need fallbacks; shedding means some users get errors | [timeouts-retries-and-backpressure](/system-design/timeouts-retries-and-backpressure) |
| High availability | SLO of 99.9%+; a single node or zone failure must not cause an outage | Replicate data; run across ≥2–3 availability zones; automated failover with fencing; stateless app tier behind a load balancer; retries + idempotency | Async replication can lose recent writes on failover; synchronous replication adds latency; multi-region adds conflict handling | [replication-and-read-consistency](/system-design/replication-and-read-consistency) |
| Latency | p99 above target; users far from the region | Cache hot data; CDN at the edge; precompute expensive results; geo-routing to nearest region; reduce round trips (batch APIs) | Every copy is a staleness and invalidation problem; multi-region writes need a conflict policy | [caching-fundamentals](/system-design/caching-fundamentals) |

## Numbers to know

Treat these as **order-of-magnitude** estimates: they tell you whether something is closer to one, ten or a thousand, not its exact benchmark score. Hardware, payload and configuration change the result, so say "roughly" and state your assumptions.

### Latency ladder

| Operation | Rough latency |
| --- | --- |
| L1 cache reference | ~1 ns |
| Main memory reference | ~100 ns |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from memory | ~10–50 µs |
| SSD random read (4 KB) | ~20–100 µs |
| Round trip within a datacenter / AZ | ~0.5 ms |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD | ~0.2–1 ms |
| Redis GET over the network | ~0.5–1 ms |
| Indexed Postgres point query | ~1–5 ms |
| HDD seek | ~5–10 ms |
| Round trip same continent | ~20–50 ms |
| Round trip cross-continent (US ↔ Europe) | ~80–150 ms |

Takeaway: memory is ~1000x faster than a network hop, and a cross-region hop costs as much as dozens of sequential in-region calls. Avoid synchronous cross-region calls on the hot path.

### Single-node throughput (rough ranges)

| Component | Rough capacity per node | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App server (stateless API) | 1k–10k+ requests/s | Depends heavily on work per request and language |
| PostgreSQL / MySQL | ~10k–50k simple writes/s; ~50k–100k+ indexed point reads/s | Large instance, small rows; complex queries are far lower |
| Redis | ~100k+ ops/s single-threaded; more with pipelining | Memory-bound: tens to hundreds of GB per node |
| Kafka broker | ~100s of MB/s; 100k–1M small messages/s | Sequential disk writes; scale by partitions |
| Cassandra / DynamoDB partition | ~1k–10k writes/s per node or partition | DynamoDB caps a single partition at ~1,000 WCU and 3,000 RCU |

### Converting DAU to QPS (worked example)

DAU means daily active users; QPS means queries or requests per second. Turn the daily total into a rate: one day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ **10^5 s**, so 1M requests/day ≈ 10 QPS on average.

- Assume 100M DAU, each viewing 20 items/day and posting 1 item/day.
- Reads: 100M × 20 = 2 × 10^9/day ÷ 10^5 ≈ **20k QPS** average; peak at ~3x ≈ **60k QPS**.
- Writes: 100M × 1 = 10^8/day ÷ 10^5 ≈ **1k QPS**; peak ≈ **3k QPS**.
- Decision: one well-tuned SQL primary can absorb 3k writes/s, but 60k reads/s argues for a cache in front of it. The read:write ratio (20:1) says optimize reads first.

### Storage per day

- 10^8 posts/day × 1 KB metadata = 100 GB/day ≈ **36 TB/year** → too big for one comfortable node within a year; plan partitioning or archiving.
- 10^7 photos/day × 2 MB = 20 TB/day → blob storage, not a database.
- Handy units: 1 KB × 1M = 1 GB; 1 KB × 1B = 1 TB; 1 MB × 1M = 1 TB.

## Technology picker cards

| Technology | Use for | Avoid for | Gotcha to mention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | Default system of record; transactions, constraints, joins, moderate scale | Multi-TB write-heavy workloads on one node without a sharding plan | Single primary for writes; replicas lag; vacuum and connection limits (use a pooler) |
| Redis | Cache, rate limiting counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), sessions, pub/sub, short locks | Primary durable store for data you cannot lose | Persistence is optional and async; pub/sub is fire-and-forget; memory is the cost driver |
| Kafka | Durable ordered event log, stream processing, decoupling producers/consumers, replay | Per-message routing/priority queues; tiny workloads | Ordering only within a partition; partition count bounds consumer parallelism; consumers must be idempotent |
| DynamoDB | Key-value / single-table access patterns at huge scale with predictable latency | Ad-hoc queries, joins, analytics | Partition key design decides everything; hot partitions throttle; secondary indexes are eventually consistent (GSIs) |
| Cassandra | Very high write throughput, wide-row time series, multi-DC replication | Transactions, joins, read-modify-write patterns | Model tables per query; tunable consistency (QUORUM); tombstones slow reads |
| Elasticsearch / OpenSearch | Full-text search, fuzzy match, faceted filters, log analytics | System of record | Near-real-time (refresh ~1 s); feed it from DB via CDC; reindexing on mapping change |
| S3 / blob storage | Files, images, video, backups, data lake | Small, frequently mutated records; low-latency lookups | Store metadata in a DB; use presigned URLs; very high durability, but per-request latency is tens of ms |
| ZooKeeper / etcd | Leader election, config, service discovery, coordination metadata | High-volume data storage | Small data only; quorum writes; use fencing tokens with any lock |
| CDN | Static assets, media, cacheable API responses near users | Personalized, per-user dynamic responses | Invalidation is slow-ish and costs money; version URLs instead of purging |
| API gateway | Auth, rate limiting, routing, TLS termination, request shaping | Business logic | Can become a single point of failure and latency hop; keep it stateless |

## Consistency decision guide

Choose consistency **per operation**, not per system.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Operation"] --> B{"Can a stale or duplicate result cost money or break an invariant?"}
    B -->|"Yes"| C["Strong: single-leader write, transaction or conditional update"]
    B -->|"No"| D{"Must the actor see their own change?"}
    D -->|"Yes"| E["Read-your-writes: primary read or version token"]
    D -->|"No"| F["Eventual: replicas, caches, async indexes"]
```

Ask the invariant question first. If staleness or duplication breaks money, inventory or uniqueness, route the operation through one authoritative writer with a transaction or conditional update. Otherwise, check whether the user who made the change must see it immediately; if so, give that session read-your-writes, and serve everyone else from eventually consistent copies.

| Operation | Choose | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booking a seat, buying the last item | Strong | Overselling costs money and trust |
| Payment / balance transfer | Strong + idempotent | Duplicates or lost updates are unacceptable |
| Unique username or short-link alias | Strong (unique constraint) | Two owners of one name is a correctness bug |
| Reading your own just-saved profile | Read-your-writes | Route to primary or wait for replica position |
| Social feed, like counts, view counts | Eventual | Seconds of lag is invisible to users |
| Search index, recommendations | Eventual | Rebuilt asynchronously from the source of truth |
| Driver location, presence | Eventual, latest-wins | Updates every few seconds supersede old ones |
| Analytics dashboards | Eventual | Minutes of lag acceptable; reconcile with batch |

Interview phrasing: "Availability for browsing; strong consistency for the booking write, enforced by a conditional update in a single database."

## Data modeling quick rules

- **Default to SQL** when you need transactions, constraints, joins, or you don't yet know all query patterns. Postgres scales further than most interview prompts need.
- **Choose NoSQL** (key-value / wide-column) when access patterns are known and simple (get by key, range by key), write volume or data size exceeds one node, and you can live without multi-row transactions.
- **Index for your queries:** every frequent `WHERE`/`ORDER BY` needs an index; composite index column order follows equality-then-range. Each index slows writes and costs storage.
- **Partition key choice:** high cardinality, evenly distributed traffic, and it should be present in most queries (so a query hits one partition). `user_id` is usually good; `country` or `created_date` alone creates hot partitions.
- **Time-ordered data:** partition by entity, sort by time (`(chat_id, message_ts)`), and bucket by time if partitions grow unbounded.
- **Denormalize deliberately:** copy data to avoid joins on hot read paths, and name who updates the copies.
- **Separate bytes from metadata:** blobs in object storage, pointers and ownership in the database.

## Common follow-up questions and crisp answers

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| What if the cache goes down? | Reads fall through to the DB; protect it with request coalescing, rate limiting and a warm standby. Size the DB to survive a cold cache or accept degraded mode. |
| How do you keep cache and DB consistent? | Write to DB, then delete the cache key; use short TTLs as a safety net; version keys for strict cases. Accept bounded staleness. |
| How do you handle a hot key? | Detect via per-key metrics; replicate hot reads (local cache, multiple copies), split hot writes into sub-keys and aggregate. |
| What happens when a shard fills up? | Use many virtual shards mapped to physical nodes (or consistent hashing) so you move whole virtual shards, not rehash everything. |
| How do you avoid duplicate processing? | At-least-once delivery plus idempotency: a key per operation stored with a unique constraint, checked in the same transaction as the effect. |
| How do you prevent double booking? | Atomic conditional update or row lock in one database; short TTL holds for checkout; never check-then-write across two calls. |
| What if a consumer falls behind? | Monitor lag; scale consumers up to partition count; shed or sample low-value work; the queue gives time, not capacity. |
| How do you do failover without split brain? | A consensus-backed leader election plus fencing tokens so the old primary's writes are rejected. |
| How do you deliver to offline users? | Persist messages first; on reconnect the client sends its last seen sequence number and fetches the gap; push notification as a nudge. |
| How do you scale WebSocket servers? | Stateless-ish gateways, a connection registry or consistent hashing for routing, pub/sub between servers, graceful drain on deploy. |
| How do you paginate a large feed? | Cursor (keyset) pagination on a stable sort key, not offset. |
| How do you handle a celebrity with 50M followers? | Hybrid fan-out: push for normal users, pull and merge for celebrities at read time. |
| How do you protect the system from a traffic spike? | Rate limit at the edge, autoscale stateless tiers, queue bursts, shed low-priority load, and serve stale cache when possible. |
| How would you migrate the schema/data live? | Expand-and-contract: dual-write, backfill, verify, switch reads, then remove the old path. |

## Anti-patterns and red flags

- Adding a cache, queue or shard without stating which requirement it serves.
- Claiming a cache or read replica will help a write-bound system.
- Claiming a queue increases sustained write throughput (it does not if consumers are the bottleneck).
- Sharding before showing one node is insufficient, or choosing a low-cardinality shard key.
- "Check then insert" for uniqueness instead of a unique constraint or conditional write.
- Distributed locks without timeouts and fencing tokens.
- Retries without timeouts, backoff, jitter or idempotency.
- Two-phase commit across microservices as the default for workflows.
- Synchronous calls to slow third parties (payments, email) on the user request path without timeouts.
- Big files flowing through application servers.
- Global strong consistency everywhere "to be safe", or eventual consistency for money.
- Ignoring failure modes: no answer for node loss, zone loss, or a dependency timing out.
- Spending 15 minutes on estimates that change no decision.
- Deep-diving one component before the end-to-end design works.

## Further reading

- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications (book site)](https://dataintensive.net/)
- [Google SRE book: Handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- [Amazon DynamoDB: partition key design](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html)
keyTakeaways: Caches, replicas and CDNs scale reads; sharding, batching and write-optimized stores scale writes, and queues only smooth write bursts.
Tie every component you add to a stated requirement and name its trade-off.
One day is about 10^5 seconds, so 1M requests per day is roughly 10 QPS on average; plan for peak at 2-3x.
Pick consistency per operation: strong for bookings, payments and uniqueness; eventual for feeds, counters and search.
Retries need timeouts, backoff with jitter and idempotency, or they make outages worse.
